overview:
Myanmar stretches down the western edge of mainland Southeast Asia, from snowy Himalayan foothills to the warm Andaman Sea. It borders India, Bangladesh, China, Laos and Thailand, and at about 677,000 km² it is roughly the size of Texas. The Irrawaddy River runs the length of the country like a spine, carrying rice barges past villages, temples and teak forests.

About 54 million people live here. Burmese is the official language, written in a rounded alphabet of circles that scribes once traced on palm leaves so the strokes would not tear them. Naypyidaw, a planned city of enormous empty highways, became the capital in 2005, replacing Yangon, which is still the largest city and home to the gold-covered Shwedagon Pagoda.

Most people are Buddhist, and monks in dark red robes collect their food in bowls each morning. Myanmar is ruled by its military, which seized power in 2021 after a short period of elected government.
landAndNature: Northern Myanmar climbs into the eastern Himalayas, where Hkakabo Razi rises above 5,800 meters and is often called Southeast Asia's highest peak. South of the mountains lies the dry central plain around Bagan and Mandalay, then the wide delta where the Irrawaddy splits into dozens of channels before reaching the sea. The monsoon soaks the coast from May to October; the Rakhine hills can receive over five meters of rain a year. Teak trees, prized for shipbuilding, grow in forests still worked by trained elephants. Tigers, clouded leopards, hoolock gibbons and the rare Irrawaddy dolphin survive here, and fishermen on Inle Lake row standing up, wrapping one leg around the oar.
peopleAndCulture: Myanmar has more than 130 ethnic groups, including the Bamar majority and the Shan, Karen, Kachin, Chin, Rakhine and Mon peoples, each with its own language and dress. Many people wear a longyi, a tube of cloth knotted at the waist, and paint their cheeks with thanaka, a pale yellow paste ground from bark that cools the skin and blocks sun. Meals center on rice with curries, fermented tea-leaf salad called laphet thoke, and mohinga, a fish-and-noodle soup eaten for breakfast. Thingyan, the water festival in April, welcomes the new year with days of soaking strangers in the street. Chinlone, a graceful team game with a woven rattan ball, has no winners or losers.
history: Pyu city-states traded along the Irrawaddy 2,000 years ago. From 1044 the kings of Bagan built more than 10,000 brick temples on one plain, thousands of which still stand. Later Burmese kingdoms fought Siam and China until Britain conquered the country in three wars between 1824 and 1885, ruling it as part of British India. Japan occupied Burma during World War II. Independence came in 1948, led by Aung San, who was assassinated months before it arrived. The army took power in 1962 and held it for decades. Elections in 2015 brought a partly civilian government, but the military seized full control again in 2021, sparking widespread protest and armed conflict. Since 2017, violence in Rakhine State has driven more than 700,000 Rohingya Muslims to flee to Bangladesh.
funFacts: The plain of Bagan holds more than 2,000 surviving temples and pagodas, built in a burst of construction lasting about 250 years.
Myanmar sets its clocks 6 hours and 30 minutes ahead of London, one of only a few countries using a half-hour offset.
Most of the world's rubies, including the prized pigeon-blood red stones, come from the Mogok valley in Myanmar.
Fishermen on Inle Lake balance on one leg at the stern and row with the other, keeping both hands free for nets.
The Shwedagon Pagoda in Yangon is covered in real gold plates and topped with thousands of diamonds.
